description_full: The Home Depot, Inc. operates as a home improvement retailer in the United States and internationally. It sells various building materials, home improvement products, lawn and garden products, and décor products, as well as facilities maintenance, repair, and operations products. The company also offers installation services for flooring, water heaters, baths, garage doors, cabinets, cabinet makeovers, countertops, sheds, furnaces and central air systems, windows, and window coverings. In addition, it provides tool and equipment rental services. The company serves consumers, such as do-it-yourself homeowners and do-it-for-me customers; and professional renovators/remodelers, general contractors, homebuilders, maintenance professionals, handymen, property managers, building service contractors and specialty tradespeople, such as electricians, landscapers, insulation installers, plumbers, painters, pool contractors, roofers, and wallboard and ceiling installers. It sells its products through websites and its mobile applications, including homedepot.com; homedepot.ca and homedepot.com.mx; blinds.com, justblinds.com, and americanblinds.com for custom window coverings; constructionresourcesusa.com or design-oriented surfaces, appliances, and architectural specialty products; thecompanystore.com, an online site for textiles and décor products; hdsupply.com for maintenance, repair, and operations products and related services; and srsdistribution.com, heritagelandscapesupplygroup.com, heritagepoolsupplygroup.com, and gms.com for roofing and building materials, landscape, and pool products; and The Home Depot stores. The Home Depot, Inc. was incorporated in 1978 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: Home Depot, Inc. (The) is a mega-cap consumer cyclical business with a $347.9B market cap on $164.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 41% against a 8% cost of capital — a 32-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 34%.

The business throws off $12.6B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.0× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.7×.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 57% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)

Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 13% operating margin runs 5pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.60x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 3.1% of sector revenue and 4.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-11.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 18% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.88, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $1.3B traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 38% in the 2020 crash, 34% in the 2022 bear market and 40% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $223 (margin of safety -57%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 19%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $173 to $291 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 24.4 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 16.6 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 27.5 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 36% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 32 covering analysts target $378 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 41% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 32pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.42).
It runs a 34% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.15x.
ROE of 110% is amplified by 8.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.3% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.0x net debt to EBITDA ($1.4B of cash against $50.8B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.8, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.5% over 3 years, 4.5% over 5 years and 6.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -5.0% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 1% of annual revenue.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 76%.
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (2.7% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 38 consecutive years, raising it 7.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 470,000 employees, each generates about $350K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 5.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $27K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.2M (12x revenue per employee).
